Isadora Duncan was an American dancer and choreographer who single-handedly created modern dance by rejecting the rigid constraints of classical ballet and returning to what she saw as the natural movement of the human body. Born in eighteen seventy-seven in San Francisco, she began her career in classical ballet but found its conventions restrictive and artistically stifling. She famously discarded pointe shoes, corsets, and tutus in favor of bare feet, a simple tunic, and movement derived from the torso and center of gravity rather than turned-out positions. She drew inspiration from Greek vases and ancient sculpture, seeking what she believed was a return to natural human movement aligned with emotion and music. She performed across Europe to great acclaim, becoming an international symbol of artistic rebellion and personal freedom, her life as controversial as her art. She created a movement vocabulary emphasizing fluidity, weight, gravity, and emotional authenticity—principles that became foundational to all modern dance that followed. She established schools in Berlin, Moscow, and Paris to preserve and transmit her technique and philosophy to future generations of dancers. Her life ended tragically in nineteen twenty-seven, but her influence on dance and on the liberation of the human body from Victorian constraints remained profound and permanent.
